"So I'm looking at that as a really good sign." Spencer said Fawcett, her family and friends are clinging to hope for a recovery. "She [Alana Stewart] doesn't want to throw out a number. And neither does Farrah. ... They're still hoping for that miracle," Spencer said. "Farrah's Story," a documentary-style program that has followed the course of her illness and showed her grueling treatment in graphic detail, aired on NBC Friday and was viewed by almost 9 million people. Fawcett and partner Ryan O'Neal watched the show together, Spencer confirmed. "Alana said it was the ultimate in bittersweet," Spencer said. "You know, they're reliving two years of hell that they've endured together." King asked Spencer whether Fawcett, who made her name a household word on the hit '70s TV series "Charlie's Angels," and O'Neal might marry. "He said you never know. He was cagey about it," Spencer said. "And, you know, I think he would in a second. He's so madly in love with her." King also had a panel of medical experts on his show to discuss Fawcett's cancer. Dr. Thomas Vogl, who at one time treated the actress in Germany, called her medical condition "very, very serious." Dr. Allyson Ocean, a medical oncologist in New York, said only about 5,000 cases of anal cancer are diagnosed in the United States yearly. Unlike Fawcett's case, it usually doesn't spread, and only about 10 to 15 percent of cases are advanced, Ocean said. Fawcett's cancer, however, is in Stage 4 and has spread to her liver. Ocean said there are various causes of anal cancer. "One of the causes is a virus called the human papilloma virus, which is a sexually transmitted virus. It seems to be more common in women, in general, outside of any viral infections. Smoking is actually a risk factor," she said. King asked Dr. Paul Song, a radiation oncologist, if he had seen Stage 4 cancer cured. "Not with anal cancer. I have seen it with other GI malignancies such as rectal cancer," Song said. "But anal cancer is a little bit more difficult to treat." Despite the bleak outlook, Song had praise for Fawcett and her documentary. "I think one of the most powerful things that Miss Fawcett did in this documentary was give patients a sense of hope and to just show how she's handled this with such courage and dignity," Song said. "You have to be absolutely honest with patients, but, you know, you don't want to strip away their hope and optimism, either. There are people, Larry, as you know, who beat the odds," Gupta said. Vogl told King he developed a close relationship with Fawcett during the time he treated her in Germany and expressed admiration for his one-time patient. "From a lot of treatments and contact and communication, I think she is extremely special, an extremely brave person," he said.

# Farrah Fawcett's Public Battle with Anal Cancer: Courage, Controversy, and Medical Reality

## A Star's Final Fight

Farrah Fawcett, the actress who became a cultural icon in the 1970s as one of television's original "Charlie's Angels," spent the final years of her life confronting a disease that few celebrities had publicly acknowledged. Diagnosed with anal cancer in 2006, Fawcett chose to document her illness in a way that would ultimately reshape public conversations about a stigmatized and poorly understood disease. She died on June 25, 2009, at age 62.

## The Diagnosis and Its Progression

Fawcett was initially diagnosed in September 2006. After undergoing treatment including chemotherapy and radiation, she was declared cancer-free in early 2007. However, the disease returned months later, having spread to her liver—advancing to Stage 4, the most severe classification, indicating metastasis to distant organs.

Rather than retreat from public view, Fawcett pursued aggressive and sometimes experimental treatments, including therapies in Germany that were not widely available in the United States. Her decision to seek alternative options abroad became a significant thread in her public story.

Produced with the help of her close friend Alana Stewart, who operated the camera through much of the filming, the documentary offered an unflinching look at chemotherapy sessions, medical consultations, and intimate moments of physical decline.

The film drew a substantial audience—reportedly nearly 9 million viewers—reflecting significant public interest in Fawcett's story and, more broadly, in a candid portrayal of terminal illness.

Many viewers and advocates credited her with removing shame from a diagnosis that patients often hesitate to discuss due to its intimate location. **Critical responses** raised ethical questions. To understand the significance of Fawcett's case, it helps to examine what medical experts have said about the disease.

### Rarity

Anal cancer is uncommon. According to the American Cancer Society, it accounts for a small fraction of gastrointestinal cancers—far rarer than colorectal cancer, with which it is often confused. The relatively low number of annual diagnoses in the United States means many people, including some patients, are unaware the disease exists as a distinct entity.

### Causes and Risk Factors

This confusion, combined with patient embarrassment about the affected area, often delays diagnosis. Experts have repeatedly stressed that timely medical evaluation of persistent symptoms is critical.

The standard treatment for localized anal cancer is a combination of chemotherapy and radiation, an approach known as the **Nigro protocol**, which has allowed many patients to avoid surgery. When caught early, the disease is often highly treatable, with favorable survival rates.

However, oncologists emphasize that prognosis changes dramatically with metastasis.
